classical_baseline: The paper frames the classical problem as adiabatic quantum optimization for finding the ground state of a problem Hamiltonian, and in the specific test case it uses the maximum independent set problem as the optimization target. It also treats perturbative crossings and small minimum gaps as the obstacle to efficient performance.
classical_baseline_quotes:
In a simple quantum adiabatic algorithm, the Hamiltonian of the system is written as
H = A(s)HB + B(s)HP ,
0 ≤s ≤1,

An important subset of quantum adiabatic algorithms
is adiabatic quantum optimization (AQO), for which the
ﬁnal Hamiltonian HP is diagonal in the computation ba-
sis. The desired ﬁnal ground state of the system is there-
fore the classical global minimum of HP .

The problem of ﬁnding an MIS in a general graph is called the maximum independent set problem,
and it is known to be NP-hard [21].

One of the mechanisms that can result in a very small
gm in AQO is when an eigenstate corresponding to some
local minima of HP (anti-) crosses that of the global
minimum near the end of the evolution [8].
classical_difficulty: The paper says the computational time depends on the minimum gap, and that very small gaps make adiabatic evolution slow. It also says that determining how the gap scales with problem size is difficult, and that perturbative crossings can make the gap exponentially small with Hamming distance between minima.
classical_difficulty_quotes:
To ensure that the system ends up in the ﬁnal ground state with high
ﬁdelity, the evolution should be very slow (adiabatic). In
a closed system, the total computation time is related to
the minimum energy gap gm between the ground state
and ﬁrst excited state of the Hamiltonian.

To determine the computational complexity of
AQC, therefore, one needs to know how gm scales with
the problem size. This is indeed not an easy task, al-
though analytic calculations have been possible for a few
special examples [2, 5–7].

In this
case, gm decreases exponentially with the Hamming dis-
tance between the two minima.

Considering random exact cover instances, it was
shown [9] that the probability of having such perturba-
tive crossings increases with problem size, which was
later numerically conﬁrmed [12].
extraction_notes: Framing is algorithmic and about AQO/MIS rather than a finance application; no finance-specific stakes are stated.
